newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude called higher on Nigeria, Iraq news.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude called higher on Nigeria, Iraq news.

text.p: NYMEX crude was called higher Tuesday on news Royal Dutch Shell Group's Nigerian unit declared a force majeure due to striking workers while Iraq breached a Western imposed "no-fly" zone.

"A lot of the call is due to two items that that were developing yesterday in Iraq and Nigeria. That coupled with the expiry (of the May crude contract) should give us a call of 15 to 20 cents higher in crude," said a New York dealer.
Heating oil and gasoline were called 0.25 to 0.50 cent a gallon higher.

"Much of the short covering nowadays is done the week of the expiry, so a lot of the expiry (short) covering should be done," said a New York crude dealer. Indeed, the May/June backwardation widened to 31 cents Monday from 24 cents Friday.
Backwardation means the contract nearer in time is more expensive than the later one.

Meanwhile, a strike by contractors that handle the berthing and loading of tankers in Nigeria has caused a delay but no cancellations of Royal Dutch Shell's Bonny light exports. Shell's bonny output is about half of the roughly 950,000 barrels per day it produces in Nigeria.
Dealers are also keeping an eye on the U.S. response to Iraq flying helicopters to Iraq's southern border with Saudi Arabia to pick up Moslem pilgrims.

The helicopter flights violated a ban by the United States and other Western powers on Iraqi flights in the area. The White House said Monday it would "respond appropriately," and some traders speculated the U.S. may try to weaken Iraq's oil-for-food accord with the United Nations.
Last December, the United Nations eased sanctions against Iraq and allowed Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months on a renewable basis in exchange for food.
Market direction after Tuesday should come in part from the American Petroleum Institute's (API) release after the market's close of oil inventory data for the week ended April 18.
Preliminary estimates from traders call for a build in crude oil and gasoline stocks of up to two million barrels while distillate stocks were seen about steady.
On Monday, May crude ended 47 cents a barrel up at $20.38. May gasoline ended 1.31 cents a gallon higher at 62.80 cents. May heating oil settled 0.80 cent a gallon higher at 55.48 cents.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
